reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities

sections.title: Purpose
sections.summary: GEC-9 gives recommended LRFD guidance for the design, analysis and testing of laterally loaded deep foundations (driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles, CFA piles) for transportation facilities, single elements and groups. It compiles FHWA, AASHTO, DOT and other published practice, is not new research and is not prescriptive. Axial design, foundation type selection and construction are outside its scope.
sections.body: The purpose of this Geotechnical Engineering Circular is to provide recommended guidance for the design, analysis and testing of laterally loaded deep foundations for transportation facilities in accordance with the Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) platform. Its audience is geotechnical, structural and highway design and construction specialists. The geotechnical and structural communities have not had a comprehensive document on this geo-structural topic, which has resulted in designs that may be overly conservative or costly. It applies to driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles and continuous flight auger (CFA) piles that resist lateral loads, often with axial loads, for new construction, rehabilitation or reconstruction; applications include single elements and groups for bridge foundations, excavation support, earth retaining structures, noise walls, sign and signal foundations, landslide repairs, vessel or vehicle impact mitigation and seismic event resistance. The GEC draws heavily on published work by FHWA, AASHTO, state and local DOTs and other publications, so it does not represent new research; its objective is a single reference for the state of the practice. The information is not prescriptive: it is current practice to be used with good engineering judgment, and does not preclude deviations based on sound local practice, demonstrated performance or testing results. Other considerations, such as selection of foundation type, axial design and testing, and foundation construction, are beyond its scope. Deep foundations may be called piles/shafts generically; "foundation" or "foundation element" means a deep foundation, and "pile" means a deep foundation element ("lateral pile analysis" is analysis of deep foundations under lateral loads). (p. 12)
key_points: LRFD guidance for design, analysis and testing of laterally loaded deep foundations (p. 12).
Covers driven piles, drilled shafts, micropiles and CFA piles, single and in groups (p. 12).
Compiles published practice; not new research and not prescriptive (p. 12).
Axial design, foundation type selection and construction are beyond its scope (p. 12).
"Pile" means any deep foundation element in the remainder of the text (p. 12).
sections.applicability: All laterally loaded deep foundation types for transportation facilities

sections.title: Background and History of Analysis of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations
sections.summary: Lateral loads come from the structure (head load and moment, largely independent of the ground) or from the ground (slope stabilization, retaining structures, lateral spread). Methods evolved from subgrade modulus (Terzaghi 1955; Hetenyi 1946), elastic (Poulos and Davis 1980) and plasticity (Broms 1964a) methods and the equivalent pile length to the nonlinear p-y method (McClelland and Focht 1958), COM624P (Wang and Reese 1993), the strain wedge method (1990s) and finite element or finite difference programs.
sections.body: Lateral loads in deep foundations occur under various conditions. In noise walls or landslide stabilization they are the principal design load; for bridge foundations they must be fully considered and in many cases control the diameter or width of the foundations. The magnitude, point of application, orientation, duration and frequency of lateral loads, and the response of the surrounding geomaterials, differ for each project. Lateral loads may come from the supported structure or from the surrounding ground. A concentrated horizontal load and/or overturning moment at the top of the element (bridge foundations, signal and sign structures, noise walls) is relatively independent of the subsurface conditions. For slope stabilization, earth retaining structures or piles subjected to lateral spread, the loads depend heavily on soil conditions and the magnitude of soil movement, which is in turn affected by the selection of the deep foundation. Methods have evolved from simple elasticity or plasticity methods using parameters from conventional tests to fully non-linear methods that may also use pile load test results (Reese and Van Impe 2001), with powerful computer programs. One of the first was the subgrade modulus concept (Terzaghi 1955): an elastic beam on an elastic foundation (Hetenyi 1946), the soil reaction depending on the deflection. Other elastic methods followed for preliminary estimates (e.g., Poulos and Davis 1980). Plasticity methods, including Broms (1964a), estimate the ultimate lateral capacity of single piles from lateral passive earth pressure. The equivalent pile length, introduced in the late 1960s for structural calculations, replaces the flexibility of the embedding soil by a fixed pile of equivalent stiffness. The nonlinear response can be considered by the p-y method (McClelland and Focht 1958), p being the lateral soil reaction along the pile and y the lateral pile displacement; the soil is a series of nonlinear springs characterized by soil type and subsurface conditions (Reese et al. 1975). It gained popularity in the 1960s and 1970s through offshore platform studies (Matlock and Reese 1961; Matlock 1970; Reese et al. 1975). COM624P (Wang and Reese 1993), developed for FHWA, was one of the first programs to use it, for a single pile/shaft under head moment and lateral load (p. 14); the p-y method is largely empirical. The strain wedge method, derived in the 1990s for a more theoretical basis, correlates soil resistance with the forces of a 3-D passive soil wedge from limit equilibrium, and the wedge strains with lateral displacement; it is run in software like the p-y method. Commercial finite element or finite difference programs handle 3-D loading, foundation geometry effects, load nonlinearity, simultaneous vertical and lateral loading, nonlinear response of concrete pile sections and pile groups. The need for this document is that current procedures are not presented in a single reference, and requirements vary by locality and standard, so general guidelines are needed for more consistent application. (pp. 13 to 14)
key_points: Head loads from the structure are relatively independent of the ground; loads from soil movement depend on it (p. 13).
Subgrade modulus (Terzaghi 1955), elastic and Broms (1964a) plasticity methods preceded nonlinear methods (p. 13).
The p-y method (McClelland and Focht 1958) models the soil as nonlinear springs; it is largely empirical (pp. 13 to 14).
COM624P (Wang and Reese 1993) was one of the first p-y programs, developed for FHWA (p. 14).
The strain wedge method (1990s) correlates resistance with a 3-D passive wedge (p. 14).
sections.applicability: Background context for understanding evolution of lateral pile analysis methods

sections.title: Literature Review
sections.summary: A literature review of state DOT, FHWA, AASHTO and other U.S. sources, comparable international sources, case histories and lateral load test studies identified gaps so that the document enhances rather than duplicates the state of the practice, including how DOTs have implemented LRFD for laterally loaded deep foundations. The report is Appendix E.
sections.body: A literature review was performed as part of developing this document, to identify gaps in the literature and existing practice so that the document would enhance, rather than duplicate, the existing state of the practice. It covered publications and guidelines by state DOTs, other U.S. sources including FHWA and AASHTO, published international sources comparable to U.S. practice, and published case histories and lateral load test studies. It provided information on how state DOTs have implemented the LRFD platform for laterally loaded deep foundation applications and how other organizations, U.S. and international, address their requirements. The literature review report is included in Appendix E. (p. 14)
key_points: Review of DOT, FHWA, AASHTO, international sources, case histories and load tests (p. 14).
Aimed to identify gaps so the GEC enhances rather than duplicates practice (p. 14).
The literature review report is Appendix E (p. 14).
sections.applicability: Background on sources and gaps addressed by GEC-9

sections.title: Organization of Manual
sections.summary: Chapters 2 to 13 cover lateral load applications and foundation type, site characterization, LRFD limit states, design process and team roles, single-element analysis, groups, extreme events, earth retention, slope stabilization, structural design, lateral load tests and construction. Appendices: A p-y curves, B design examples, C example load test, D guide specification for lateral load tests, E literature review.
sections.body: The remainder of the document: Chapter 2, lateral load applications and selection of deep foundation type, including excluded types; Chapter 3, geotechnical characterization (investigation, testing and soil and rock parameters); Chapter 4, LRFD design requirements and limit states, load and resistance factors; Chapter 5, design process and design team roles of geotechnical and structural engineers; Chapter 6, analysis of single laterally loaded elements, simplified and computer methods, their applicability and other design considerations; Chapter 7, lateral analysis of groups (groups versus single foundations, spacing, group effects, frame action); Chapter 8, design for extreme events such as seismic and vessel impact loading; Chapter 9, earth retention structures (wall types, earth pressures, geotechnical strengths, deformations); Chapter 10, slope stabilization (earth loads and soil-pile models); Chapter 11, structural design and performance (shear and moments, foundation types, connections, foundations in rock with high shear near the top of rock); Chapter 12, lateral load tests (use, limitations, alternatives, types, instrumentation, data analysis, reports); Chapter 13, construction considerations that may affect lateral capacity; then References. Appendix A gives example p-y curves and parameters; Appendix B detailed design examples; Appendix C example load test results and interpretation (p. 16); Appendix D a guide specification for lateral load tests; Appendix E the literature review report on current practice. (pp. 15 to 16)
key_points: Chapters 2 to 13 run from applications and site characterization to load tests and construction (p. 15).
Appendix A: example p-y curves and parameters (p. 16).
Appendix B: design examples; Appendix C: example load test interpretation (p. 16).
Appendix D: guide specification for lateral load tests; Appendix E: literature review (p. 16).
sections.applicability: Navigation guide for practitioners using GEC-9
